analysis.one_liner: Requires the Navy to keep 12 aircraft carriers instead of 11.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed federal law to require the Navy to maintain at least 12 operational aircraft carriers instead of the 11 currently required. Since a new Ford-class carrier costs roughly $13 billion and takes years to build, the bill amounted to a standing order for at least one additional nuclear supercarrier. It never advanced past a subcommittee referral and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Nuclear shipbuilders — principally Huntington Ingalls' Newport News yard, the only U.S. yard that builds nuclear carriers — and their supplier chains would gain a guaranteed multibillion-dollar order. Navy planners who argue the current 11-carrier fleet is stretched too thin would also get the fleet size they have sought.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends Title 10 of U.S. Code to raise the statutory minimum from 11 to 12 operational aircraft carriers, effective September 30, 2023 [S3].

The bill's findings argue the Navy has 'significant carrier gaps' in the Central and Pacific commands, that deployments have lengthened while the fleet shrank, and that truncated training 'increases sailor risk' [S3].
The findings also argue that designing a smaller alternative to the Ford-class carrier is not cost-beneficial, effectively endorsing continued Ford-class procurement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: U.S. taxpayers, since each additional Ford-class carrier costs on the order of $13 billion and the annual carrier operating and crewing costs run into the hundreds of millions, all competing with other defense and domestic spending. Taxpayers also bear the risk of cost overruns that have marked the Ford-class program.

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates a fleet size without identifying offsets, so the extra carrier — roughly $13 billion for construction alone — would either add to defense spending or force cuts elsewhere [S3].

The Navy's own stated requirement, as quoted in the bill, is 2 carriers deployed and 3 ready to deploy within 90 days; whether that requires a 12th hull is a contested force-structure judgment, not a settled fact [S3].
The bill was a one-line fleet-size mandate with no funding mechanism, and it drew no cosponsors in over two years [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest case for the bill is operational: an 11-carrier fleet facing rising deployment lengths and maintenance backlogs could genuinely benefit from a 12th hull, and the bill's findings document that strain [S3]. But the bill was pure mandate with no money attached: the marginal carrier would cost roughly $13 billion to build plus large annual crewing and maintenance costs, and the bill's text explicitly steers procurement toward the Ford class — a program known for cost growth. Given that a single-carrier increase could arguably have been handled in the annual defense authorization process where tradeoffs are weighed, a standalone statutory floor was a blunt instrument whose main certain beneficiary was the shipbuilding industrial base.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Armed Services Committee and then to its Seapower subcommittee, never received a markup or a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. K. Michael Conaway (R-TX) introduced the bill on January 22, 2019 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Armed Services on January 22, 2019, and to the Subcommittee on Seapower and Projection Forces on January 24, 2019 [S5].
No further action occurred through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers, in the narrow sense that no additional multibillion-dollar carrier mandate was enacted without offsets. Nothing changed: the Navy's statutory floor remained 11 carriers, and the shipbuilding industry gained no guaranteed order from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; no new carrier mandate enacted

for.name: Rep. K. Michael Conaway
for.role: Sponsor, House Armed Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case for a 12-carrier fleet in its findings.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a markup
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee and its Seapower subcommittee for the full two-year Congress without acting on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors, so no partisan split is visible in the record; the sponsor was a Republican on the Armed Services Committee [S1, S4].

industries.note: The only U.S. yard that builds nuclear carriers would have gained a guaranteed roughly $13 billion order plus decades of maintenance work from the 12-carrier floor. Its gain would come directly from federal taxpayers with no offset identified in the bill.

industries.industry: Defense electronics, aircraft, and naval supplier chains
industries.note: Carriers carry air wings and thousands of supplier contracts; an additional hull means additional procurement across the defense industrial base, paid for by taxpayers. The bill's findings explicitly endorse continuing Ford-class procurement rather than a cheaper alternative design.

An extra supercarrier would cost on the order of $13 billion to build plus substantial annual operating costs, either adding to the deficit or crowding out other spending. The bill proposed the mandate without any funding source.
